summary:
Nariño department stands under Colombia's national framework. The source inventory contains no Nariño-specific legal provisions, incidents, or enforcement practice; the findings below are national in scope and are recorded here as they bear on a visitor to this department.

Colombia recorded 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and 41 trans women killed over the course of 2023. Eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. These are national totals, not Nariño figures.

On 5 April 2025 a trans woman, Sara Millerey, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; the assault was filmed and the video circulated widely. She died the following afternoon. No arrests had been made as of 14 April 2025, although police questioned local residents. President Gustavo Petro directed authorities to investigate urgently, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

Armed groups continue to threaten and displace trans people despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Caquetá department, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she fled at night after hiding for a week. 'Social cleansing' flyers distributed on the street and through WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets.

Discrimination restricts trans women in Colombia largely to hairdressing or sex work. Earlier fatal attacks documented in reporting include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while asleep, and killings in victims' homes and in a hairdresser.
tangentialFactors:
The national figures cited above are raw counts with no per-capita or population denominator given in the sources; they rank nothing about Nariño relative to other departments.

Caquetá and Antioquia, where the documented threats and the Millerey killing occurred, are separate departments from Nariño. The inventory does not establish that the same armed-group flyer campaigns or threat patterns operate in Nariño.
localsOnly: No Nariño-specific enforcement practice, local institutions, or resident-facing obligations were identified in the inventory. Residents of Nariño stand under the national legal framework and the national protection machinery described in the parent record.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns or kill-list flyers have circulated in Nariño is unresolved; the inventory documents such campaigns only in Caquetá and, per the parent record, Guajira.

Nariño's own homicide or threat statistics for trans people are not sourced here. The 13-trans-people and 41-trans-women figures are national totals and cannot be attributed to this department.

Local notary or registry practice in Nariño on gender-marker changes and on registration of marriages performed abroad is not sourced in this inventory.
